# Proof of the Corrected Claim

The claim as stated is false if we adopt the standard convention (as in the given definitions) that the natural numbers $\N$ include $0$. The generalized sum $\sum \set{v_n : n \in \N}$ includes the term for $n=0$, whereas the series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty v_n$ explicitly omits it. For example, if we let $v_0 = 1$ and $v_n = 0$ for all $n \ge 1$, with $r = 1$, the generalized sum is absolutely net convergent to $1$, but the series starting at $n=1$ is absolutely convergent to $0$, not $1$.

We prove the corrected claim, which aligns the index sets:
**Corrected Claim:** Let $V$ be a Banach space, $\sequence{v_n}_{n \in \N}$ a sequence in $V$, and $r \ge 0$. The generalized sum $\sum \set{v_n : n \in \N}$ is absolutely net convergent to $r$ if and only if the series $\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_n$ is absolutely convergent to $r$.

By definition, absolute net convergence of the generalized sum to $r$ means the net of finite sums of norms, $\left(\sum_{n \in F} \norm{v_n}\right)_{F \in \mathcal{F}(\N)}$, converges to $r$, where $\mathcal{F}(\N)$ is the directed set of finite subsets of $\N$ ordered by inclusion. Absolute convergence of the series to $r$ means the sequence of partial sums of norms, $S_N = \sum_{n=0}^N \norm{v_n}$, converges to $r$ as $N \to \infty$.

## (1) implies (2')
Assume the generalized sum is absolutely net convergent to $r$. Let $\epsilon > 0$. By net convergence, there exists a finite subset $F_0 \subset \N$ such that for all finite subsets $F \supset F_0$, we have $\left| \sum_{n \in F} \norm{v_n} - r \right| < \epsilon$.
Let $N_0 = \max(F_0)$ (if $F_0$ is empty, let $N_0 = 0$). For any $N \ge N_0$, consider the set $F_N = \{0, 1, \ldots, N\}$. Since $N \ge \max(F_0)$, we have $F_0 \subseteq F_N$.
Applying the net convergence condition to the finite subset $F_N$, we obtain $\left| \sum_{n=0}^N \norm{v_n} - r \right| = \left| \sum_{n \in F_N} \norm{v_n} - r \right| < \epsilon$.
This implies $\lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{n=0}^N \norm{v_n} = r$, so the series $\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_n$ is absolutely convergent to $r$.

## (2') implies (1)
Assume the series $\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_n$ is absolutely convergent to $r$. This means $\lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{n=0}^N \norm{v_n} = r$.
Since $\norm{v_n} \ge 0$ for all $n$, the sequence of partial sums $S_N = \sum_{n=0}^N \norm{v_n}$ is monotonically non-decreasing. Therefore, the limit is also the supremum: $\sup_{N \ge 0} \sum_{n=0}^N \norm{v_n} = r$.
For any finite subset $F \subset \N$, let $N = \max(F)$ (or $0$ if $F$ is empty). Then $F \subseteq \{0, 1, \ldots, N\}$. Since the norms are non-negative, $\sum_{n \in F} \norm{v_n} \le \sum_{n=0}^N \norm{v_n} \le r$. Thus, for all finite $F$, $\sum_{n \in F} \norm{v_n} \le r$.
To show net convergence, let $\epsilon > 0$. Since $\lim_{N \to \infty} S_N = r$, there exists $N_0 \ge 0$ such that $r - \sum_{n=0}^{N_0} \norm{v_n} < \epsilon$.
Let $F_0 = \{0, 1, \ldots, N_0\}$. For any finite subset $F \supset F_0$, we have $\sum_{n \in F} \norm{v_n} \ge \sum_{n \in F_0} \norm{v_n} > r - \epsilon$.
Combining this with $\sum_{n \in F} \norm{v_n} \le r$, we get $r - \epsilon < \sum_{n \in F} \norm{v_n} \le r$, which means $\left| \sum_{n \in F} \norm{v_n} - r \right| < \epsilon$.
This proves that the net of finite partial sums converges to $r$, so the generalized sum is absolutely net convergent to $r$.
